key_insight: In thin 316L foil laser keyhole welding, rising line energy drives keyhole instability that nucleates holes, which then grow rapidly once their length approaches the sheet thickness.
engineering_relevance: The work identifies practical energy thresholds for keeping seams continuous versus avoiding perforation, directly informing process windows for thin-sheet overlap welding.
method: High-speed imaging of bead-on-plate welding on 200 µm foils representing 100 µm overlap joints
Tracked keyhole instability, hole nucleation, and subsequent hole growth under increasing line energy
Used a Young-Laplace-based geometric stability criterion to relate hole growth to sheet thickness
evidence_signal: The abstract reports continuous seams up to about 7 kJ/m, hole formation beyond that range, and cutting dominance above about 12 kJ/m, with holes expanding at roughly 0.8–1.2 m/s over 1–3 ms.
watch_item: The stability criterion is geometry- and material-specific, so thresholds may shift with alloy, thickness, shielding, and laser setup.
paper_title: Rupture and growth of holes in the melt pool during laser keyhole welding of thin sheets
